Android from the foundation · Start here

The one idea behind everything

Your app doesn't control its own life. Another process decides, and tells your app by sending messages to its main thread.

The problem

Why does Android kill your screen on rotation? Why can a background app die without onDestroy()? Why does one slow line of code freeze the whole UI? These look like separate rules to memorise. They aren't: they all follow from one idea about who is in charge.

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The four characters

Every puzzle in this course uses these four. Learn the picture once and you can reason about the rest.

  • Your app's process: your house. It runs your code, but it doesn't decide when things happen.
  • system_server: the town hall. One long-running Android process that keeps the register of apps, screens, windows and permissions.
  • The kernel, with Binder: the post office. The only thing that can carry data between processes.
  • The main thread: the one clerk at your front desk, handling one letter at a time.

Who decides that your Activity should be created?

Right. system_server decides. Binder only carries the message, and your app is told.

Can system_server call a method on your Activity object directly?

Right. It lives in a different process and can't touch your app's memory, so the request travels through Binder.

Right. The message lands in your main thread's inbox, and the main thread runs your callback when it gets there.

What you now know

system_server decides → Binder carries the message → your main thread receives it → your callback runs. You don't call onCreate(); you get called.
